name: SONiC
vendor: SONiC Foundation (Linux Foundation), created at Microsoft
summary: Software for Open Networking in the Cloud: a Linux-based network operating system for data centre switches, built by Microsoft for Azure, that runs on hardware from many vendors through a common chip interface.
intro: A data centre switch is a forwarding chip (an ASIC) plus software that decides what to program into it. Traditionally both came from one vendor. SONiC is that software as open source, a network operating system based on Linux that runs on switches from many vendors and chips. It reaches the hardware through the Switch Abstraction Interface (SAI), an API for controlling forwarding chips in a vendor-independent way, which chip makers implement in their own SDKs. The build tree has platform support for Broadcom, Marvell, NVIDIA (Mellanox), Cisco, Centec and others, plus a virtual switch for testing.

Inside, each function runs in its own Docker container, and they share state through a Redis database rather than calling each other. CONFIG_DB holds configuration such as ports, VLANs and BGP neighbours, loaded from `/etc/sonic/config_db.json` at boot; APPL_DB holds what applications want, such as routes; ASIC_DB holds the same state in a form ready for the chip. When BGP, run by FRR in the `bgp` container, learns a route, `fpmsyncd` writes it to APPL_DB, `orchagent` in the Switch State Service (swss) translates it into ASIC_DB entries, and `syncd` calls the SAI to program the chip. Other containers run link aggregation (teamd), LLDP, SNMP and platform monitoring, so one can be restarted or upgraded without touching the rest.

SONiC is cut twice a year, in May and November, as branches named after year and month; 202605 is the latest. In October 2026 Network World cited Gartner’s estimate that about 2,500 organisations run SONiC in production, roughly a third of them enterprises, and 650 Group’s forecast of more than $5 billion in SONiC-based data centre switching revenue in 2026, driven largely by AI clusters. It has been hosted at the Linux Foundation since April 2022, under the SONiC Foundation.
strengths: One operating system across switches from many vendors and chip makers, so automation, tooling and skills carry over
Proven at hyperscale: built for and run in Azure’s data centres, and the basis of commercial distributions from switch vendors
Modular containers and a Redis state database make it easy to inspect, extend and restart one function at a time
Vendor-neutral governance at the Linux Foundation, with an Apache 2.0 licence and backing from Microsoft, Google, NVIDIA, Broadcom, Cisco and Arista
limits: Needs network engineers comfortable with Linux, containers and automation; Dell’Oro says operating it requires a specialised skill set
Hardware support depends on each chip vendor’s SAI implementation and each switch’s platform drivers, so check that your exact model is supported
Shaped by hyperscale cloud and AI data centres: the roadmap centres on their fabrics, not on campus or branch networks
Community releases are source branches and images without support; for that, enterprises turn to the distributions that switch vendors increasingly offer

story: Microsoft wanted the software on Azure’s switches to stop depending on who made the hardware, so that it could choose hardware freely and change software at its own pace. Its first step was SAI, a common API to switch chips, which the Open Compute Project (OCP) accepted from Microsoft in July 2015. On March 9, 2016, at the OCP summit, Microsoft open-sourced SONiC, the Linux-based switch software built on SAI, with contributions from Arista, Broadcom, Dell and Mellanox, and proposed it for OCP.

SONiC spread from Azure to other cloud providers and to switch vendors, who began selling it on their own hardware. By 2022 it ran on more than 100 different switches. On April 14, 2022 it moved to the Linux Foundation, which adopted a technical charter for the SONiC Foundation that day; OCP kept working on hardware and on specifications such as SAI.

AI clusters then sped up its adoption. From around 2025 the community realigned its roadmap around AI data centre workloads, adding SRv6-based load balancing, packet trimming for congestion recovery and high-frequency telemetry, and Dell’Oro expects sales of SONiC switches for AI scale-out networks to grow by more than 50% a year through 2030. New members, including Lenovo in October 2026, kept joining the foundation.

choices.choice: A common interface to the chip (SAI)
choices.why: Defining one API for forwarding chips let the same software run on any vendor’s hardware that implements it, so Azure could buy switches on price and features rather than software.
Putting each function in its own container and passing state through a database decouples them, so one can crash, restart or be upgraded without bringing the switch down.
Using Linux and an existing open-source routing stack let operators reuse familiar tools and contribute fixes instead of waiting for a vendor.
